title: Digital Tongues
welcome_lead: From SMS to TikTok captions, contemporary change accelerates. Map the newest sediments of English.
meta_desc: Contemporary language change, internet English, neologisms and Crystal's perspective at A-Level.
final_note: You have audited the bleeding edge of English — change has not slowed, only re-platformed.

concepts.def: A newly coined word or expression (selfie, doomscroll, ick).
Abbreviation pronounced letter by letter (LOL, BTW, OMG), proliferating in digital discourse.
David Crystal argues internet English is a new variety, neither speech nor writing but a third medium, and language is healthier than ever.
Halliday's view (SFL) that language changes to meet the communicative needs of its users.
Chen's S-curve describes how innovations spread slowly at first, accelerate, then plateau.
Charles Hockett's theory that small random changes accumulate without overall direction.

walkthroughs.body_html:
David Crystal (2001) argues that computer-mediated communication is not the death of English but its expansion into a new medium with its own conventions — Netspeak.

Initialisms, emojis and hashtags emerge to handle real-time multimodal exchange, enriching rather than degrading the language.

Chen's S-curve plots adopters against time. Early adopters use a new form sparingly; the curve steepens as the form goes mainstream; it plateaus as the change becomes standard.

Google as a verb followed this trajectory — peripheral in 2001, ubiquitous by 2010, standard by 2020.

Halliday's systemic functional linguistics holds that language is a resource shaped by use. Change happens because speakers need to mean new things — economic, technological, social.

The rise of they as a singular gender-neutral pronoun illustrates a functional response to evolving identity vocabulary.
